parts.title: Booking a holiday cottage

turns.text: Good morning, Greenhollow Cottages, Joanne Pickering speaking. How can I help?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Hello. I'd like to book a cottage for a week this summer, please. It's for me, my wife and our two kids.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Lovely. I'll just fill in a booking form as we go. Could I start with your surname?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Yes, it's Brereton. That's B-R-E-R-E-T-O-N. First name Martin.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thank you, Mr Brereton. And when were you hoping to come?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Well, we'd planned to arrive on Saturday the 12th of July, but my son's got a football tournament that weekend. So it'll have to be the Saturday after, the 19th.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Right, arriving Saturday the 19th of July and leaving the following Saturday. Did you have a particular cottage in mind?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: My wife spotted one on your website called Bramble Cottage. She thought it looked lovely.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Ah, I'm sorry, Bramble's already booked for that week. But there's another one on the same farm that's very similar. It's called Heron Cottage, like the bird. That's H-E-R-O-N.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Heron Cottage. OK. And how many bedrooms has it got? We need at least two.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Well, the website still says two, but the owners have just converted the loft, so there are actually three now. Two doubles and a small single.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Oh, that's even better. My son and daughter can have a room each, then. That'll save a few arguments!
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: I'm sure! Now, will you be bringing any pets? Heron Cottage is one of our pet-friendly ones.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Yes, we'll bring our dog. The kids wanted to bring their rabbit too, but my mother's offered to look after it while we're away.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Very sensible. So that's just the one animal. Now, the price for that week. Most of the summer it's £595, but the 19th falls in the school holidays, so it goes up to £640, I'm afraid.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: £640. Hmm, a bit more than we'd budgeted for, but it sounds worth it. Let's go ahead.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Great. Is there anything extra you'll need in the cottage?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Yes, actually. We'll bring our own high chair, because we've got a travel one, but could you provide a cot? Our daughter's only eighteen months.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: No problem at all. I'll put that on the form, and there's no charge for it.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Brilliant. And what's included in the price? I don't want to pack things we don't need.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Well, electricity and heating are covered. Bed linen's provided, of course, and so are towels, so you can leave those at home. The one thing that isn't included is firewood for the stove, but you can buy a basket from the farm shop.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: That's fine, I doubt we'll need a fire in July anyway. How does payment work?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We take a deposit of £150 today, by card. Then the rest is due six weeks before you arrive. Some agencies give you until four weeks before, but we're a bit earlier than that, so do make a note of it.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Six weeks. OK, I'll put a reminder in my phone. And could you tell me how to find the place? It's quite remote, isn't it?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: It is a bit. You'll come into the village of Ashby Wold on the main road. Drive straight through, past the pub on your right, and then take the first left just after the church.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Past the pub, then left after the church. Got it.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Then follow that lane for about a mile and you'll see the farm. Please don't park in the farmyard, because the tractors need to get through. There's plenty of space next to the barn, so leave your car there.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Next to the barn. Right. And how do we get the key? We probably won't arrive until about seven in the evening.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's fine. There's a key safe on the wall by the front door. Your code is 4718. The old code was printed in some of our leaflets, but it's been changed, so only use the one I've just given you.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: 4718. Brilliant. Thanks so much for your help.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: You're welcome, Mr Brereton. Now, if I could just take your card details for the deposit.
turns.speaker: agent

parts.title: Welcome to Wattle Point Coastal Reserve

turns.text: G'day everyone, and welcome to Wattle Point Coastal Reserve. My name's Bronwyn Cassidy, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you head off, I'll give you a quick idea of where everything is, and then tell you what's on today. You should all have a map – if not, grab one from the box by the door.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Right. So we're standing outside the visitor centre, which is on your left as you come in through the main gate and walk north along the main track. Now, some of you will remember that the café used to be in here with us. Well, it's moved. It's now directly across the track from the visitor centre, so it's on your right as you walk in. They do great coffee and homemade scones, by the way.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: If you carry on north past the café, the next thing you come to on the right-hand side is the picnic area. There are tables, a shade shelter and a couple of free gas barbecues, which you're welcome to use. And straight opposite that, on the left, is a small hut – that's the first-aid post. If anyone gets hurt or stung, that's where to go.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: A bit further up, there's a narrower track branching off to the left, and that takes you to the lagoon. Just before you reach the water, you'll see a little brick building on the near side of the lagoon – the south side. That's the pump house, and it's kept locked, so don't worry about it.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Keep following the track round the edge of the lagoon, and on the far shore, the northern side, you'll find the bird hide. It's well worth sitting in there for a while, especially early in the morning.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Now, back on the main track. At the top it turns right, towards the ocean. As you walk east along that last stretch, the first building on your left is the staff cottage. That's private, I'm afraid – it's where our volunteers stay. On your right, though, opposite the cottage, is the Discovery Room, which has some great displays on local marine life, including a real whale skeleton. It's open from nine until five, and entry's free.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: And then, right at the very end of the track, just before you step onto the sand, there's the lookout on your left. It's a tall wooden tower, so you can't really miss it. From the top you can often spot dolphins, and whales from about June onwards.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: OK, so that's the layout. Now, what's actually happening today? We run a guided walk every Saturday at ten – sorry, half past ten.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Usually it's a rock-pool walk, but the tide's too high this morning for that. So instead, one of our volunteers, Greg, is going to take you through the dunes and talk about the native plants that hold the sand together. Meet him here at the visitor centre.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: For the kids, there's an activity in the Discovery Room at two o'clock. The poster outside says shell painting, but we've actually decided against that, because we don't want to encourage people to take shells off the beach. Instead, the children will be using microscopes to look at sand and seaweed up close. They love it, honestly.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: If you'd like a swim, the beach is patrolled by surf lifesavers today from ten till four, and we ask you to stay between the red and yellow flags. Please don't swim in the lagoon, by the way. That's never allowed, because it's a breeding area for the birds.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: The café's open as usual, but it's closing early today – at half past two instead of four – because the staff have a training session. So if you're planning to have lunch there, don't leave it too late. And just so you know, they've stopped taking cash, so you'll need a card.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Now, one warning. Last week we had a few complaints about the boardwalk down to the beach being slippery, but that's been fixed. What you do need to watch out for is the magpies. It's nesting season, and they've been swooping on people along the lagoon track, so wear a hat or just walk through quickly.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: Finally, before you go home. You don't need to sign out at the gate any more – we used to ask people to do that, but not now. And the map's yours to keep. What we'd really appreciate is if you'd fill in a bird-sighting card – there's a tray of them by the door – and drop it in the box at the visitor centre.
turns.speaker: ranger

turns.text: It really helps us keep track of numbers. Right, that's it from me. Enjoy your day!
turns.speaker: ranger

parts.title: Planning a presentation on city noise

turns.text: So, Marcus, we really need to lock in the plan for our presentation today. It's due in three weeks, and we haven't even agreed on sources.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I know. First, though, I feel like we should explain to Professor Novak why we didn't take her suggestion. She proposed light pollution, remember?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. I don't think she'll mind, though. And it's not as if we turned it down because there wasn't enough material. There's loads on light pollution.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: True. Honestly, it was the construction outside my apartment that settled it. They've been drilling for the new light rail line since September, and I haven't slept past seven in weeks.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I remember you complaining. Okay, sources. I think the World Health Organization guidelines on environmental noise have to be at the center of everything.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Isn't that report kind of old, though? I think it came out in 2018.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: It's a few years old, sure, but almost every study I've found refers back to it. So it's really the obvious place to start.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. Some of the appendices are pretty technical, though.
turns.speaker: student_b

parts.title: The history of food preservation

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Helen Ashworth, and today's lecture is about something we rarely stop to think about: how people have kept food from going off. I'm going to look at four methods, drying, salting, canning and refrigeration. And, more importantly, I'll look at how each one changed what people actually ate.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's start with drying, which is almost certainly the oldest method. The idea is simple: take the moisture out, and food lasts much longer. Now, people often assume the earliest drying was done over a fire. Actually, that's smoking, which came later. The very first drying relied on the sun and the wind, and in a dry climate that was really all you needed.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Drying had a huge effect on trade. Dried fruit kept for months, so it could be carried enormous distances. Grapes were dried, of course, to make raisins. But in the ancient Mediterranean, the fruit that travelled furthest was the fig. Merchants carried it right across the region, and it turned up in places where nobody could possibly grow it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Drying also made food much lighter, because most of the weight in fresh food is just water. That made it ideal for people who were always on the move. Hunters used it, certainly. But the group that depended on it most were herders, who followed their animals from one pasture to the next and simply couldn't carry heavy loads.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, let's move on to salting. Salt works by drawing water out of food, and without water, bacteria can't grow. So salted meat or fish could last a whole winter, or a long sea voyage.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: In northern Europe, salting fish was enormously important. You might expect me to say cod, and cod certainly mattered later on. But in the Middle Ages, the fish that fed much of northern Europe was the herring. It was caught in huge numbers in the Baltic and the North Sea and packed into barrels of salt.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Of course, salted food is very salty, and cooks had to deal with that. The usual approach was to soak the meat or fish overnight before cooking it. Most people just used water. But if you look at recipes from wealthier households, they often recommend soaking it in milk, which was thought to give a softer, milder result.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, canning is a much more recent invention, and it has a rather interesting origin. At the end of the eighteenth century, the French government wanted a better way to feed its army and navy. So it offered a prize to anyone who could find a reliable way of preserving food. It was eventually won by a confectioner called Nicolas Appert, in 1809, sorry, 1810.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What surprises many students is that Appert didn't use cans at all. His food was sealed inside glass bottles and then heated in boiling water. Metal cans, made of iron coated in tin, were introduced in Britain a little later, partly because they didn't break so easily.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Early tins were thick and heavy, and the can opener hadn't been invented yet. So how did people get them open? Well, soldiers sometimes used a knife, or even a bayonet. But the instructions printed on some early cans actually told you to use a hammer and a chisel. Not exactly convenient!
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: By the late nineteenth century, though, canned food was cheap, and that really changed diets. Tinned meat and fish became everyday foods for working families. And exotic fruit reached ordinary homes for the first time. Peaches were popular, but the real symbol of this was tinned pineapple, which became a favourite treat in Britain, especially at Sunday tea.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, refrigeration. Before mechanical fridges, the only way to keep things cold was natural ice. Wealthy families stored it in icehouses, often underground. In the nineteenth century, ice was imported into Britain on a large scale. Some of the early shipments came from America, but most of Britain's ice actually came from Norway, where it was cut from frozen lakes in winter.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The real breakthrough, though, was refrigerated shipping. In 1880, sorry, 1882, a ship arrived in London from New Zealand carrying frozen meat that was still perfectly good after more than three months at sea. Frozen beef from Argentina followed later, but that first cargo was mostly mutton, and New Zealand lamb soon became a regular part of the British diet.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And when fridges finally arrived in ordinary kitchens in the twentieth century, people no longer had to shop for fresh food every single day. So, each method didn't just keep food safe. It changed what ended up on the plate. Next week, we'll look at how the supermarket changed things all over again.
turns.speaker: lecturer

parts.title: Changes to rubbish and recycling collections

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Graham Pennington, the waste services officer at Wexley Town Council. From the 3rd of March, there are some fairly big changes coming to the way we collect your rubbish and recycling, so I'll explain what's changing, when, and what you need to do.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: So, first of all, why are we doing this? A lot of people assume it's because of complaints, but actually we get very few. No, the main reason is money. The tax we pay on every tonne of rubbish that goes to landfill has gone up again, and frankly, that cost ends up on everyone's council tax bill, which nobody wants. So that's one thing.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: The other reason is that our agreement with the old collection company runs out this spring. We've signed with a new firm, and they work in a slightly different way. Now, you may have read in the paper that new government rules forced us into this. That's not quite right, actually. Those rules don't come in for another two years. And no, we haven't had any trouble finding drivers, unlike some councils.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Right, so what's going to arrive on your doorstep? During February, every household will get a printed collection calendar through the letterbox. Please stick it on the fridge, because the days and weeks will be different for some of you. We did think about sending everyone a free compost bin as well, but the budget just didn't stretch that far, I'm afraid.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: In the same envelope, you'll also find a set of stickers. They go on the lids of your bins and show, with pictures, what belongs in each one. Now, I know some people were hoping for brand-new wheelie bins, but the ones you've already got are perfectly fine, so we're keeping those. And there's no separate guide to the website. Everything's already online.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Now, with any change like this, a few bins are bound to get missed in the first few weeks. If that happens to you, please don't ring the depot, because the phone lines there just can't cope. Instead, report it on the council website, ideally by the end of the following day. It only takes a couple of minutes, and you'll get a reference number by email.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: And this is important: keep your bin out at the kerb. Don't wheel it back in, because the crew will come back round, usually within forty-eight hours. There's no need to drive it to the tip yourself, either. Oh, and please don't pile extra bags next to it. They won't be taken, and they attract foxes.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Right, let's go through the main types of waste one at a time. Starting with ordinary household rubbish, that's the black bin. At the moment it's emptied every fortnight, but from March that'll go out to once every three weeks. I know that sounds like a long time, but if you're recycling properly, it really shouldn't fill up.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: That's possible because food waste is getting a better service. Up to now, it's gone in with the garden waste every two weeks. From March, your food caddy will be picked up every single week, on the same day as your other bins. Most of what makes a black bin smell is food, so this should really help.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Garden waste is the one that's caused the most debate. It's been free until now, but from March there'll be a yearly fee of £45, sorry, £42, for the brown bin. If you don't sign up, it simply won't be emptied. The collection day stays the same, though, so that's one thing you won't have to remember.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Next, glass bottles and jars. These used to go loose in the blue bin with everything else, and broken glass was causing real problems at the sorting plant. So from now on, they'll need to go in a box of their own, which you can pick up free from the library. You don't have to rinse them, by the way. Just make sure they're empty.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Batteries are new. We've never collected them before, but now you can put them out with your recycling. Just pop them in a clear plastic bag, a sandwich bag is fine, and leave it on top of your blue bin lid, where the crew can spot it.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Clothes and other textiles are going the other way, I'm afraid. The new company can't take them from the kerbside, so from March, please use the clothing banks in the supermarket car parks, or give them to a charity shop.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: And finally, large items like sofas, mattresses and fridges. You still need to book these online, just as before, but we've managed to bring the price down. It used to be £35 for up to three items, and it's now £25.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: So that's everything. The full details are on the council website. Thanks very much for listening.
turns.speaker: officer

turns.text: Hi Liam. Have you had a chance to look at Dr Sutherland's feedback on our field report?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I read it on the bus this morning. It's better than I expected, actually. We got a credit, and she reckons we could get a distinction if we fix a few things in the final version.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Oh, that's a relief. I was sure she'd rave about the photos, given how long we spent taking them on the rock platform at Long Reef.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: She mentioned them, but only in passing. And the introduction got a tick, but nothing more. What she really praised was the way we explained how we laid out the quadrats and counted everything. She said another student could repeat our survey exactly, just from reading that section.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's great, because I rewrote that bit about three times. So what about the results? I thought that section was pretty solid.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Mostly, yes. I thought she might complain that we'd shown the same data in a table and a graph, but she was fine with that. The problem is the bar charts. We left the units off the axes, so the reader can't tell if we mean snails per quadrat or per square metre.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Oh no. Well, at least that's quick to fix. Did she say anything about the captions?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: She said they were clear, so we can leave those alone.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good. And the discussion? I was a bit worried it went on too long.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, she said the length was about right. And she was happy with the sources, too. Eight journal articles is plenty at this level. The real issue is that we never actually say whether our hypothesis was supported. We set it up in the introduction, that there'd be more snails closer to the low-water mark, and then we never come back to it.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right, so we need a paragraph that answers it directly. Yes or no, and why.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. Then there's the species list in the appendix. She questioned whether it should be there at all.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Well, I don't want to delete it. It took us ages to put together. Could we add a photo of each species to make it more useful?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That'd double the length of the report. Her suggestion was to turn it into a table in the results, because really it's part of our data, not extra information.
turns.speaker: student_b

parts.title: How desert plants survive heat and drought

turns.text: Okay, good morning, everyone. Last week we looked at how plants cope with cold, and today we're going to the other extreme: deserts. I'll cover four things: roots, leaves, water storage, and the timing of growth. And I'll use some plants you've probably heard of.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, roots first. Desert plants tend to follow one of two strategies, and the first is to go deep. The mesquite tree is the classic example. Its main root, the taproot, has been found more than forty, sorry, more than fifty meters down.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: For a long time, people assumed it was chasing whatever rainwater soaked down through the sand. But rain rarely gets that far. What the mesquite is really after is groundwater, the permanent supply sitting far below the surface. Once it taps into that, it can stay green through the worst droughts.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second strategy is the opposite: stay shallow and spread out. Most cacti have roots just a few centimeters below the surface, but they can extend in every direction for several meters. When a storm does come, they soak up water before it evaporates.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And here's the clever part. After rain, a cactus grows extra fine roots, which we call rain roots, and it doesn't take days, as you might expect. They appear within a few hours. Then, once the soil dries out again, those rain roots simply die off, so the plant isn't wasting energy on them.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. Let's move on to leaves. Leaves are a problem in the desert, because every leaf loses water through its surface. So many desert plants have tiny leaves, or none at all.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: In cacti, the spines are actually leaves that have changed shape over time. Now, most people think spines are just there for defense, to stop animals eating the plant. They do that, of course. But what surprises my students is that a thick covering of spines also casts shade on the stem, which can lower its surface temperature by several degrees.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Other plants keep their leaves but protect them. Take the creosote bush, which covers huge areas of the American Southwest. You might expect its leaves to have a waxy layer, like a lot of plants do. In fact, they're coated in a sticky resin, which slows water loss and also tastes terrible to insects.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And then there's the ocotillo, which takes a completely different approach. For most of the year it looks like a bundle of dead sticks. But within days of a good rain, it's covered in small green leaves, and when the soil dries, it drops them again.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: You'll read in some books that it does this about three times a year, but that's really a dry-year figure. In a wet year, it can grow a new set of leaves as many as six times.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: One more thing about leaves and stems. Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores called stomata, but every time those pores open, water escapes. Most plants open them during the day, when they're making food. Many desert plants, including cacti and agaves, use a system called CAM, so they keep their pores shut in the heat of the day and open them at night, when it's cooler.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, water storage. The best-known example has to be the saguaro, the giant cactus you see in every Western movie. Its stem has deep folds, or pleats, running from top to bottom. After rain, those pleats open out so the stem can swell, a bit like an accordion.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: A large saguaro can hold well over a thousand liters. So how long can it last on that? You'll sometimes hear people claim two years, and honestly, that's an exaggeration. A full year without rain is a more realistic figure, and that's still remarkable.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Its smaller relative, the barrel cactus, has a nickname: the compass barrel. That's because older plants lean in one direction. There's a popular story that they point north, so lost hikers can find their way. Actually, it's the opposite. They lean toward the south, and the reason seems to be that it keeps the strongest sun off the growing tip.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's leave North America for a moment. In southern Africa there are tiny plants called living stones, which look exactly like pebbles. Their thick leaves store water, and most of each leaf is buried underground, where it's cooler. So how do they get light? Well, the top of each leaf has a clear patch that works like a window, letting sunlight down inside.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, timing. Some plants don't really try to survive the drought at all. Desert annuals, the small wildflowers, spend the dry periods as seeds in the soil. And they can wait there not just months, or even a few years, but decades, until conditions are right.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Many seeds have a chemical in their coat that stops them sprouting, and only a heavy soaking washes it away. A light shower isn't enough, which protects them from starting too early. Then they race through their whole life cycle in a few weeks.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: You might think summer would be the main season for this, since some deserts get summer thunderstorms. But in the Sonoran Desert, the most famous displays follow the winter rains. So if you want to see the desert covered in flowers, the best time to visit is spring.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, for next week, please read chapter nine. And think about which of today's strategies you'd expect to find in plants on a rocky coastline.
turns.speaker: lecturer
